Nell, publisher; John Dick, printer) -- FOUR ISSUES: Vol. I Nos. 2-5, January 7, 14, 21 and 28, 1848. Slugs NS_1848-01-07, NS_1848-01-14, NS_1848-01-21, NS_1848-01-28; 4 pages each; source scans Digital Howard @ Howard University, Black Press Archives. Extraction rule per Michiko (2026-08-05, same as extractions64): capture ALL events and the people at them, and any organization with a named membership, anywhere -- New York, Boston, Rochester, Philadelphia included; skip editorial/opinion matter, reprinted literature and general antislavery argument unless a named body or gathering is involved. OCR: 7-column broadsheets OCR'd column by column; all rosters below were additionally verified by reading the page images directly (150dpi renders, column crops), not from OCR alone. The standing List of Agents on page 1 is identical across all four issues and is recorded once under NS_1848-01-07; it adds two agents to the December 3 list (Elias Doty, Macedon; Amarancy Paine, Providence). Pages with no qualifying content: 01-07 p3-p4 (Thompson speech continuation, ads), 01-14 p3 (essays/selections), 01-21 p4 (British & Foreign A.S. Society report extracts, no roster), 01-28 p3 (religious reprint, ads, National Era prospectus).

articles.headline: Speech of Geo. Thompson, Esq., M.P., on Free Trade with India
articles.summary: From the London Mercury. 'The meeting being organized, Francis Carnac Brown, Esq., addressed the assembly: Ladies and gentlemen -- I thank you for the honor you have conferred upon me, in electing me to preside over this very large meeting...' Brown explains his eight years' acquaintance with George Thompson since returning from India, and introduces Thompson's long speech urging free-grown East India cotton as the peaceful and infallible remedy against American slavery. The speech fills much of pages 1 and 4.

articles.headline: The National Bazaar
articles.summary: 'It was our happiness last week to attend the exhibition of anti-slavery industry, elegance, and beauty, held in Boston... our expectations were very high; but, on entering, they were more than gratified.' An editorial visit to the fourteenth National Anti-Slavery Bazaar in Boston, describing the evergreen-decked hall, the evening addresses by well-known anti-slavery speakers, and defending the women conducting the fair against the charge of playing into the hands of aristocracy. The writer says it was his lot to make the last anti-slavery speech in Faneuil Hall on the last night of the old year.

articles.headline: Movements
articles.summary: 'Since the appearance of the first number we have been actively [holding] public meetings in various parts... and the State of Massachusetts...' Notes a meeting in Mendon on the 4th with friend Remond, held in the school house after other doors were closed, two meetings the next day, and meetings by C. L. Remond elsewhere; reports that co-laborer M. R. Delany, with his family in Pittsburgh, will probably remain absent for the present winter and hold meetings in Cincinnati and the State of Ohio.

articles.headline: Correspondence
articles.summary: 'We give our readers the following letters, at the hazard of incurring the charge of egotism...' Letters welcoming the North Star: Gerrit Smith (Peterboro', Dec. 8, 1847), enclosing deeds of forty acres each (a quarter of the same lot) to Frederick Douglass and William C. Nell under his land-gift to the colored inhabitants of New York -- he has also given lots to Mr. C. L. Remond and Mr. W. W. Brown, and divided one lot amongst escaped slaves, viz: Henry Bibb, and others, Lewis, Milton, and Cyrus; Samuel J. May (Syracuse, Dec. 9); a Quaker friend signing Isaac C. Kenyon; Abner H. Francis (Buffalo, Dec. 17); James Sperry (Henrietta, Dec. 11); J. W. C. Pennington (Hartford, Ct., Dec. 27); an unsigned Friend's letter from Seekonk, Mass., 12th Mo. 17th, 1847; and an extract signed Abby L. Brigden, from the correspondence of a devoted laborer in Ohio.

articles.headline: Notices; Notices of New Publications
articles.summary: Publisher's and lecture notices: Charles Lenox Remond and Frederick Douglass will hold a meeting in Victor on Monday evening, 10th Jan.; J. C. Hathaway is now making a tour in Massachusetts and will receive subscribers for the North Star -- he will visit Boston, New Bedford, Providence and Fall River, and return in time to attend the fair at West Winfield; Henry Watson is now travelling in the State of Rhode Island, and is authorised to receive subscribers -- Mr. Watson has experienced the wrongs of slavery in his own person; Frederick Douglass will deliver an Anti-Slavery Lecture next Sunday afternoon at two o'clock in the Wesleyan Methodist Church, Main Street. New publications noticed: A Letter to the Citizens of the United States, by Rev. Theodore Parker; Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (eleventh thousand); A Lecture delivered before the Female Anti-Slavery Society of Salem, at Lyceum Hall, Nov. 14, 1847, by William W. Brown, a fugitive slave; Narrative of William W. Brown, now passing through a second edition.

articles.headline: Mr. Hale in the Senate
articles.summary: From the Emancipator. 'We are able to give the following interesting particulars in regard to the presentation (on the 22d) of the memorial of the yearly meeting of anti-slavery friends in Indiana. Here follows the petition...' The account gives the memorial in full, Mr. Hale's remarks on presenting it, the objections of Mr. Johnson of Maryland, Mr. Calhoun and Mr. Butler, and the yea-and-nay vote (33 to 9) by which the motion to receive the petition was laid upon the table. Mr. Hale also presented a petition of David T. Burr and citizens of Pennsylvania for such an alteration of the constitution and laws as should abolish slavery throughout the Union.

articles.headline: Report of the Committee on a National Press
articles.summary: From the proceedings of the National Convention of Colored People (Troy, October 1847). 'The Committee on a National press and printing establishment for the people of color, made the following report on the importance and practicability of such an undertaking: It being admitted that the colored people of the United States are pledged, before the world and in the face of heaven, to struggle manfully for advancement in civil and social life, it is clear that our own efforts must mainly, if not entirely, produce such advancement...' The report urges 'a printing press, a copious supply of type, a full and complete establishment, wholly controlled by colored men,' and sets out the ten-point plan adopted by the Committee of seven, naming the Executive Committee of eleven (see event). Signed J. McCune Smith, G. B. Wilson, Wm. H. Topp.

articles.headline: Report of the Committee on Abolition
articles.summary: From the Troy convention proceedings. 'The committee appointed to draft a report respecting the best means of abolishing slavery and destroying caste in the United States, beg leave most respectfully to report... they have arrived at the conclusion that the best means of abolishing slavery is the proclamation of truth, and that the best means of destroying caste is the mental, moral and industrial improvement of our people.' The report disapproves of any appeal to bloodshed, and closes with resolutions to 'AGITATE!! AGITATE!!!' till our rights are restored. Signed Frederick Douglass, Alexander Crummell, John Lyle, Thos. Van Rensselaer.

articles.headline: The Colored Convention -- Report of the Committee on Education
articles.summary: 'The committee appointed to make a report on the state and wants of educational privileges of the colored people, and the educational advantages of colored persons in the United States, beg to report, that they have endeavored to consider the subject presented to them... with that care and thoughtfulness demanded by so important a subject.' The report urges mental culture as a primeval duty, proposes that the Convention place before the colored people of the United States the founding of a college as its leading object, and recommends a committee of twenty-five with full powers to devise a plan and obtain subscriptions. Signed Alex. Crummell, Jas. M'Cune Smith, P. G. Smith; the committee of twenty-five appointed by the Convention is printed in full (see event).

articles.headline: Valedictory of the Mystery -- union with the North Star
articles.summary: The publishers of the Mystery (Pittsburgh) announce their retirement: 'The Mystery is still afloat, with the solemn promise of the Publishers, to keep her tiding the broad waters of destiny, doing battle in the great struggle for liberty and right, elevation and equality, God and humanity, as in days bygone.' The Publishing Committee, 'faithful to their trust, and prompt to a man,' are commended; the editor leaves the Mystery for a union with 'the far famed and world renowned Frederick Douglass, as a co-laborer in the cause of our oppressed brethren, by the publication of a large and capacious paper, the North Star, in Rochester, N.Y.' -- M. R. Delany's valedictory on merging his Pittsburgh paper into the North Star.

articles.headline: George B. Vashon refused admission to the Pittsburgh bar
articles.summary: From the Pittsburgh Telegraph. An account of the refusal of the Committee of the Pittsburgh bar to examine Mr. Vashon for admission 'because his complexion was a shade darker than their own.' On application to the Court for a rule on the Committee directing them to examine him, the Judge refused the rule. 'There was no pretence that the applicant is not of excellent moral character, of gentlemanly deportment and well qualified for admission... A drop of African blood flowed in his veins, and he was refused admission to the Bar. He now leaves his native city, to take up his abode among strangers, expatriated by the cruel prejudices of his fellow citizens.' (See NS_1848-01-28 p2 for his admission in New York and intended removal to Hayti.)

articles.headline: Notice -- Remond and Douglass at Penn Yan
articles.summary: 'Charles Lenox Remond and Frederick Douglass will hold several meetings during Saturday and Sunday, 22d and 23d Jan., in Penn Yan.'

articles.headline: The Fourteenth National Anti-Slavery Bazaar
articles.summary: Report of the fourteenth National Anti-Slavery Bazaar at Faneuil Hall, Boston, signed Maria Weston Chapman. 'Thanks to your constancy, the receipts of the Bazaar were FOUR THOUSAND THREE HUNDRED DOLLARS...' The report describes the transformation of Faneuil Hall into a 'cathedral' of evergreens, the towns represented, the tables from the congregations of Rev. James Freeman Clarke and Rev. Theodore Parker, the fifty friends who united to purchase the Cork table-cover which fell to the lot of John T. Hilton, and the donations of British and Irish friends; it closes with an appeal for the coming year. (See event for the persons named.)

articles.headline: Editorial Correspondence -- M. R. Delany from Pittsburgh
articles.author: M. R. Delany
articles.summary: 'Dear Douglass: -- I am still in Pittsburgh, getting ready, as fast as possible, to start out on my Western tour for the North Star...' Delany reports that the proprietors of the Mystery, his old paper, are making industrious efforts to sustain it; that the 'Pittsburgh Saturday Visiter,' a new antislavery paper recently commenced by 'the distinguished and eccentric Mrs. Swisshelm,' is engaging attention; and that on 'next Tuesday, the 18th,' a Levee is to be held in Philo Hall for the benefit of the Mystery -- 'This is the divine work of the Ladies. God bless them!' He also remarks on the fearful steamboat explosions. Signed M. R. D.

articles.headline: Colored lawyers -- George B. Vashon, Robert Morris and Macon B. Allen
articles.summary: Notice, with New York intelligence from the Tribune/Telegraph, that 'Geo. B. Vashon' was admitted 'as Attorney and Counsellor of the Supreme Court' of New York on examination showing perfect knowledge of the rudiments and familiar acquaintance with Blackstone and Kent; he intends to practice in Hayti, where a letter of recommendation will let him plead without being sneered at. The editors correct the claim that this is the first admission of a colored lawyer: in Massachusetts two colored lawyers have long been in practice -- Robert Morris, who acquired his excellence of character and business habits in the office of Loring, Esq., Master in Chancery, and Macon B. Allen, who passed the ordeal of a rigid examination at the Cumberland bar (Maine) and holds the office of Justice of the Peace under the appointment of the Governor. 'To Massachusetts, then, belongs the honor of first extending its hand of encouragement to those colored young men aspiring to legal lore.'

articles.headline: Letter of David Ruggles on the National Press
articles.author: David Ruggles
articles.summary: Communication dated Northampton, Jan. 1, 1848, addressed 'Friends Douglass & Delany.' Ruggles hails the North Star as 'a beacon light of liberty' and argues that while our brethren of the South are slaves to slaveholders, 'we, of the North, are slaves to' public sentiment; he urges the necessity of the 'National Press' called for by the Troy Convention, until which there is sincere devotedness on the part of the whole people to sustain the most able, free and independent press ever established and conducted by colored men in this country. Signed 'Yours for Human Freedom, DAVID RUGGLES.'

articles.headline: Notices
articles.summary: Local notices: 'We were compelled for the want of room to omit some of the sayings at the Printers' Festival; but as there were many good sentiments proposed, we insert the following: By P. Fogg -- The war spirit -- tamed by the press.' Grateful acknowledgment of valuable documents from the Hon. J. G. [Palfrey?] of the House of Representatives (surname imperfect in the copy). 'Benjamin R. Foster is our authorized Agent for Rochester and its vicinity.' The Liberty Minstrel by Geo. W. Clark for sale at the office.

events.name: Fourth Annual Meeting of the Western New York Anti-Slavery Society
events.description: Pursuant to notice, the Society convened at Minerva Hall, Rochester, on 'Monday, December 12th' as printed (December 12, 1847 fell on a Sunday; the Monday was the 13th). Joseph C. Hathaway in the chair, Wm. C. Nell appointed Secretary pro tem. Committees were chosen on Business (Frederick Douglass, Sarah D. Fish, Nelson Bostwick, Mary Hallowell, R. G. Murray, Phebe Hathaway, Charles L. Remond), Finance (Wm. R. Hallowell, Lewis Burtis, Henry Bush, Giles B. Stebbins) and Nomination (Benjamin Fish, Sarah Burtis, Eliza Parker, G. B. Stebbins, Isaac Post), the latter reporting a list of officers unanimously adopted: President Joseph C. Hathaway of Farmington; Vice-Presidents Henry Bush (Rochester), Wm. G. Parker (West Walworth), A. L. P--t (Victor; surname smudged, Post or Peat), Elias L. Platt (Bath), Thos. McClintock (Waterloo), Nathan Marvel (Port Byron); Corresponding Secretary Giles B. Stebbins; Recording Secretary William C. Nell; Treasurer Henry Bush; and an Executive Committee of thirty-eight (all listed below). Resolutions thanked the agents of the American Anti-Slavery Society, commended the National Anti-Slavery Standard, welcomed 'our distinguished friends and well-tried fellow laborers, Frederick Douglass, M. R. Delany and Wm. C. Nell, editors and publishers of the North Star,' hailed the appearance of the North Star, hailed free-grown British India cotton and George Thompson's recent effort before his constituency, denounced the New York demonstration of sympathy with Pope Pius IX while war is carried on in Mexico, and mourned the deaths of Rev. Charles Van Loon and of James C. Fuller, friends of the slave.

events.name: Great Anti-Slavery Meeting at Minerva Hall
events.description: Pursuant to a call extensively circulated through the city, a large audience convened in Minerva Hall on Sunday morning, [December] 19th, 'for the purpose of considering the sin of American Slavery, and our duties, as Christians, towards its utter annihilation.' Joseph C. Hathaway was called to the chair, and Giles B. Stebbins and Wm. C. Nell appointed Secretaries. Prayer was offered by Rev. Mr. Howard. Frederick Douglass offered resolutions declaring that in the simple act of slaveholding are comprehended the crimes of theft, robbery and murder; during discussion through the day and evening Douglass detailed the church's influence against the liberation of the slave, remarking that preaching for the slave was a paramount duty, inasmuch as 'a man is of more value than a sheep.' Giles B. Stebbins censured the clergy for coldness and indifference; C. L. Remond briefly commented on the resolutions; J. C. Hathaway presented a graphic picture of the injuries heaped upon the free colored people of this land and the slaves on the southern plantations. After remarks in further support by M. D. Codding, L. Burtis, and others, the resolutions were unanimously adopted, the meeting united in an anti-slavery hymn, three cheers for liberty were given, and the meeting adjourned. Signed J. C. Hathaway, Pres't, Wm. C. Nell, Sec'y.

events.name: Anti-Slavery Fair at Minerva Hall (Western New York fair)
events.description: Report (signed 'W. C. N.', William C. Nell) of the anti-slavery fair held at Minerva Hall, Rochester, in December 1847, whose 'last day and evening, the 18th, was an auspicious one.' The spacious hall was well filled, the ladies all vieing with each other in ways and means to induce visitors to buy; two bands at intervals discoursed 'Liberty Notes.' William C. Bloss, Esq., and Frederick Douglass occupied the rostrum to the hearty acceptance of all. The report praises the labors and sacrifices of the anti-slavery women and closes with the language of Frederika Bremer. The Rochester Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society committee's acknowledgment of contributions to this fair appears in the January 14 issue.
attendees: occupied the rostrum on the closing evening, December 18
occupied the rostrum on the closing evening, December 18

events.name: Rochester Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society annual meeting (announced)
events.location: House of Mr. J. Kedzie, No. 35 North Fitzhugh Street, Rochester, New York
events.description: Notice: 'The Rochester Ladies Anti-Slavery Society will hold its Annual Meeting on Thursday, 13th January, at two o'clock afternoon, at the house of Mr. J. Kedzie, No. 35, North Fitzhugh Street. Members and friends of this Society are earnestly requested to attend.'
attendees: annual meeting to be held at his house, 35 North Fitzhugh Street

events.name: Lecture by William W. Brown before the Female Anti-Slavery Society of Salem
events.description: Noticed among new publications: 'A Lecture delivered before the Female Anti-Slavery Society of Salem, at Lyceum Hall, Nov. 14, 1847. By William W. Brown, a fugitive slave.' The editors add: 'We have received a copy of this able lecture, recently delivered by our friend and brother, William W. Brown. Mr. Brown is well known in Western New York as an efficient laborer in the anti-slavery field. He declared his independence of slavery but a few years since.'
attendees: delivered the lecture before the Female Anti-Slavery Society of Salem; a fugitive slave

events.name: Public meeting on free trade with India, addressed by George Thompson, M.P.
events.description: From the London Mercury: a very large public meeting on free trade with India, at which Francis Carnac Brown, Esq., was elected to preside; he described his eight years' cooperation with George Thompson on questions relating to India since Thompson's return from the United States. George Thompson, M.P. for the Tower Hamlets, delivered the speech of the evening, arguing that the free cultivation of cotton in British India is a simple, peaceful and infallible remedy against American slavery. The Western New York Anti-Slavery Society's resolutions in this same issue extend acknowledgments to Thompson 'for his recent eloquent and able effort before his constituency.'
attendees: elected to preside over the meeting
M.P. for the Tower Hamlets; delivered the speech on free trade with India

events.name: Memorial of the Yearly Meeting of Anti-Slavery Friends in Indiana, presented in the United States Senate
events.location: United States Senate, Washington; the yearly meeting held at Newport, Wayne County, Indiana
events.description: Mr. Hale presented (December 22) the memorial of the yearly meeting of anti-slavery Friends in Indiana -- described in debate as 'the yearly meeting of Friends at Newport, Wayne county, Indiana' -- praying Congress to use all the means in its power to put an immediate termination to the war with Mexico, and to exercise the powers of the government to put an immediate termination to slavery with all its horrid consequences, so far as those powers extend. The memorial was 'Signed on behalf of the meeting, Walter Edgerton, Rebecca Edgerton, Clerks.' Mr. Hale urged that the petition be received; Mr. Johnson of Maryland, Mr. Calhoun and Mr. Butler objected; the motion to receive was laid on the table, yeas 33 (Messrs. Allen, Ashley, Atchison, Atherton, Badger, Bell, Berrien, Bradbury, Breese, Bright, Butler, Calhoun, Cass, Davis of Mississippi, Dickinson, Dix, Downs, Fairfield, Felch, Foote, Hunter, Johnson of Maryland, Johnson of Louisiana, Mangum, Mason, Niles, Rusk, Sevier, Spruance, Sturgeon, Turney, Westcott, Yulee), nays 9 (Messrs. Baldwin, Clarke, Corwin, Greene, Hale, Miller, Phelps, Underwood, Upham).
attendees: Clerk, signed the memorial on behalf of the yearly meeting of anti-slavery Friends in Indiana
Clerk, signed the memorial on behalf of the yearly meeting of anti-slavery Friends in Indiana

events.name: Anti-slavery lecture by Frederick Douglass at the Wesleyan Methodist meeting house ('The Meeting on Main Street')
events.location: Wesleyan Methodist meeting house, Main Street, Rochester, New York
events.description: 'In the meeting house of the Wesleyan Methodists, on Main street... a small band of men and women meet to hear the Gospel of Freedom and Love for all.' An anti-slavery lecture was given by Frederick Douglass last Sunday afternoon [January 9], notwithstanding the severity of the storm. After prayer by Mr. Benson, the clergyman of the society, and the singing of an anti-slavery hymn, Mr. Douglass spoke for an hour or more to a respectable audience on the nature of real Christianity, and toward the conclusion, with tears from many eyes, gave a simple narrative of some of his own experience of cruel prejudice and ill treatment as a colored man. His sentiments were warmly responded to by the minister and a number of the members of the society. Signed 'S.'
attendees: clergyman of the Wesleyan Methodist society; offered prayer and responded warmly

events.name: Rochester Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society -- committee acknowledgment for the recent fair
events.description: 'The committee of the Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society gratefully acknowledge the receipt of valuable and saleable articles from friends in the country for the recent fair.' Contributions came from the anti-slavery women of Ledyard; from Walworth and Farmington (sewing circles); from Waterloo (books, perfumery); from Williamson, 'the result of the labors of a little company of workers in our good cause,' forwarded with an excuse for personal non-attendance owing to the fatal illness of one of their number, whose decease in the flower of her days will be lamented by all (see the death notice of Eliza A. Cooper of Williamson, NS_1848-01-21 p3); from a friend in Mt. Morris; from Bath, by donation of goods and personal presence; from Port Byron, a box of useful and fancy goods during the fair; and an offering from a friend in Wisconsin, formerly a co-laborer here at home. Signed 'In behalf of the committee, C. A. F. S.' (initials as printed).
attendees: signed the acknowledgment in behalf of the committee of the Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society (initials as printed)

events.name: Western New York Anti-Slavery Society Executive Committee meeting (called)
events.location: House of Isaac Post, 36 Sophia Street, Rochester, New York
events.description: Notice: 'The Executive Committee are requested to meet at the house of Isaac Post, 36, Sophia Street, Rochester, on Tuesday evening, January 18th, at 7 o'clock. A full attendance is specially important. Per order, W. C. Nell, Sec.'
attendees: Executive Committee to meet at his house, 36 Sophia Street

events.name: Franklin's Birth-Day -- Rochester printers' celebration (announced)
events.description: 'The Printers of Rochester will commemorate the one hundred and forty-second anniversary of the birth-day of Franklin, on Monday evening, the 17th inst. They respectfully tender an invitation to their fellow craftsmen in the surrounding towns to unite with them on the occasion; also, to the retired printers of the city. The celebration will be held at the Irving House, kept by Col. T. W. Haskell, a veteran printer.' Friends intending to attend are to notify the Chairman of the Committee of Arrangements by Friday. Signed James Vick, Jr., Ch'n Com. Arrangements. (The full report of the festival appears in NS_1848-01-21 p3.)
attendees: keeper of the Irving House, a veteran printer

events.name: Executive Committee on the National Press for the Free Colored People of the United States
events.location: New York City (meetings to take place in the city of New York); appointed by the National Convention at Troy, October 1847
events.description: Under the plan adopted by the Committee of seven appointed by the Troy National Convention with full power, 'there shall be an Executive of eleven persons, to be denominated, The Executive Committee on the National Press for the Free Colored People of the United States, viz: Massachusetts -- Leonard Collins, James Mars; Connecticut -- Amos G. Beman, James W. C. Pennington; Kentucky -- Andrew Jackson; New York -- J. McCune Smith, Chas. B. Ray, Alex. Crummell; New Jersey -- E. [P.?] Rogers (initial before Rogers partly cut in the copy); Pennsylvania -- Andrew Purnell, George B. Vachon [as printed; i.e. Vashon]; of which Committee James McCune Smith, of New York, shall be Chairman, and Amos G. Beman, of Connecticut, Secretary.' Members residing in New York City form a Finance Committee depositing funds in the New York Seaman's Bank for Savings; the Committee holds stated meetings once in six months and publishes its accounts; 'the Rev. J. W. C. Pennington, of Connecticut, shall be the Foreign Agent of the National Press'; home agents receive twenty per cent and the foreign agent thirty per cent on collections. The report is signed J. McCune Smith, G. B. Wilson, Wm. H. Topp.

events.name: Committee on the best means of abolishing slavery and destroying caste (Troy convention)
events.location: National Convention of Colored People, Troy, New York (report printed in this issue)
events.description: The committee appointed by the Troy National Convention 'to draft a report respecting the best means of abolishing slavery and destroying caste in the United States' reported that the best means of abolishing slavery is the proclamation of truth, and the best means of destroying caste the mental, moral and industrial improvement of the people; it disapproved of any counsel of insurrection and bloodshed as 'the perfection of folly,' recommended a committee of one to draft a fuller report for the next National Convention, and closed with resolutions pledging to 'AGITATE!! events.name: Committee of twenty-five on the establishment of a college for colored young men (Colored National Convention)
events.location: Appointed by the National Convention of Colored People, Troy, New York; members in Troy, Albany, New York, Philadelphia, Hartford and New Haven
events.description: The Report of the Committee on Education (signed Alex. Crummell, Jas. M'Cune Smith, P. G. Smith) resolved 'That this Convention places before the colored people of the United States, the founding of a college, as its leading and most important object,' and that a committee of twenty-five be appointed with full powers to devise a plan, obtain subscriptions and designate proper and capable persons to conduct such an institution, sans caste but not exclusive, reporting to the convention at its next annual session. 'The following committee was appointed by the Convention, in accordance with the recommendation of the report: Troy -- Wm. Rich. Albany -- Wm. H. Topp, Stephen Myers, Moses Jackson. New York -- Wm. A. Tyson, Charles L. Reason, James M'Cune Smith, George T. Downing, John J. Zuille, Albro Lyons, Samuel E. Cornish, Charles B. Ray, Alexander Crummell, Patrick H. Reason, U. B. Vidal, Christopher Rush, Edward V. Clark. Philadelphia -- Joseph Cassey, Wm. Douglass, James J. G. Bias, Stephen Smith, Frederick A. Hinton. Hartford -- J. W. C. Pennington. New Haven -- Joseph Brown, Amos G. Beman.' (Joseph Cassey died within weeks; see his death notice, NS_1848-01-21 p3.)

events.name: Third Annual Festival of the Printers of Rochester (Franklin's birthday)
events.description: 'Third Annual Festival of the Printers of Rochester, held at the Irving House, January 17, 1848,' commemorating the birth of Franklin. The tables were loaded in the style peculiar to that house of Haskell; thanks are given to the Committee of Arrangements, Jas. Vick jr., Chairman, Geo. W. Wiss [surname as printed; unclear] and H. K. Wilson; the room was decorated with flags, pictures, evergreens and a transparency of Franklin prepared and presented by D. P. Newell. P. Canfield was called upon to preside, and E. Shepard, A. Strong, and J. M. Patterson acted as Vice Presidents; during the whole Festival the Band of Adams discoursed music. Twelve regular toasts (Franklin, Our Country, The Union, State of New York, the President, the Governor, The Press, Printers -- 'Mechanics of the mind,' the Heroes of '76, Franklin and Morse, Our Common Schools, the Deceased Brothers of the Craft) were followed by an ode by R. L. B. Clarke and a long list of volunteer toasts. Frederick Douglass gave: 'Gentlemen of the Rochester Press -- Promoters of knowledge, lovers of Liberty, foes of ignorance, dispensers of prejudice [sic] -- may you continue to give the world noble examples by a free and intelligent union of black and white.' events.name: Anti-Slavery Fair at West Winfield (announced)
events.description: 'Anti-Slavery Fair at West Winfield, on January 26th and 27th, 1848. -- The friends of the slave are invited to make preparations for our next Fair, to be held at the time above mentioned. There is no time to be lost. The slave is still toiling, toiling, toiling, -- hopeless, helpless, desolate. -- Woman, -- aye, a million of women are even now given up to the tender mercies of the palefaced oppressor...' Charles Lenox Remond, E. D. Hudson, Lewis Hayden, J. C. Hathaway, and other speakers will be present. Signed by sixteen women: Dolly Thomas, Miranda A. E. Green, Sarah Guild, Phebe Backus, Hannah Bucklin, Laura Eldred, Emeline Murdock, Julia Ann Exton, Henrietta Bisby, Laura Turner, Eveline Rider, Sophloro Thomas (as printed; possibly Sophrona), Alpha Thomas, Laura Colburn, Susan Brown, Amanda Harding. An editorial note adds that the editors expect to be present at this fair on the 26th and 27th.

events.name: Death of Eliza A. Cooper of Williamson
events.description: Death notice: 'In Williamson, Wayne county, New York, on the morning of the 21st of December, of typhus fever, Eliza A., youngest daughter of Griffith M. and Eliza M. Cooper, aged 20 years 6 months and 8 days.' She is evidently the member of the Williamson sewing company whose fatal illness was reported in the Rochester Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society fair acknowledgment (NS_1848-01-14 p2); her father Griffith M. Cooper sat on the Western New York Anti-Slavery Society executive committee.
attendees: died December 21, 1847, of typhus fever, aged 20 years 6 months 8 days

events.name: Death of Joseph Cassey of Philadelphia
events.description: Death notice, from the Pennsylvania Freeman: 'On Monday night at 12 o'clock, of apoplexy, Joseph Cassey, of this city, in the 59th year of his age. Mr. Cassey was a most respectable citizen, and in his worldly circumstances one of the most prosperous and wealthy of the oppressed class in Philadelphia. He was the first agent of the Liberator in this city, and in the earlier stages of the cause, was among Mr. Garrison's most zealous co-laborers and effective friends. He has left an amiable and interesting family, consisting of a wife and six children, to mourn his loss.' Cassey had just been named to the Philadelphia section of the colored college committee of twenty-five printed on page 1 of this same issue.
attendees: died of apoplexy in his 59th year; first Philadelphia agent of the Liberator; among Garrison's most zealous co-laborers
named in the notice as one whose earliest co-laborers included Cassey (printed as Mr. Garrison)

events.name: Fourteenth National Anti-Slavery Bazaar, Boston
events.description: Full report of the fourteenth National Anti-Slavery Bazaar, held in Faneuil Hall and closing at the new year; receipts four thousand three hundred dollars. The foremost of the thirty towns cooperating were Cambridge, Worcester, Lynn, Plymouth, Dedham, New Bedford, Concord, Weymouth, Hingham and Brookfield, with effectual aid also from the State and city of New York and contributions from the friends in Western New York. Visitors could look on 'Garrison, and Phillips, and Francis Jackson, Edmund Quincy, and Henry C. [Wright], and Samuel May, and Pillsbury, Foster, and Stone, and Doug[lass], Buffum, and Parker, and Cha[pman]' (line ends worn). A few weeks before the opening, the Boston Female Anti-Slavery Society held its annual meeting and commended the Bazaar to friendly congregations; members of the congregations of Rev. James Freeman Clarke and Rev. Theodore Parker each furnished a table, both ministers cheering the effort. Fifty friends united to raise fifty dollars for the Cork table-cover, which fell to the lot of John T. Hilton, 'a man of color, a devoted abolitionist, and a member of the executive board of the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society from the earliest days of the cause,' who had promptly aided Wm. Lloyd Garrison at the commencement of the Liberator. Dr. Nichol and Rev. Mr. Hincks, editor of the London Inquirer, were welcomed; vocal and instrumental music was furnished by members of Mr. Channing's congregation through the exertions of Mr. Withington, and Mr. Chickering sent an admirable piano forte from his celebrated manufactory. Among donors acknowledged: the Webbs, the Haughtons and the Allens of Dublin; the Jenningses, the Mannixes, the Varinas, the Roches, the Beamishes and the Whites of Cork; Esther Bright of Rochdale, sister of John Bright; Mrs. Moore, Mrs. Cobden and Miss Woolley of Manchester; the Nicholsons and the Peiles; Mr. Lupton of Leeds; the Browns and the Trends [as printed] of Bridgewater; and helpers Messrs. Smith and Weston, Jenkins, Wellington of Lexington, Brigham of Abington, and friends of Providence, Bridgewater and West Roxbury. Signed Maria Weston Chapman. The reference in the report to the anti-slavery women of thirty towns and the Liberty Bell accompanies an appeal for the Liberator and the National Anti-Slavery Standard.

events.name: American Baptist Free Mission Society -- special meeting of the Board of Trustees and officer roster
events.description: Address 'To the Baptists of the United States, and the Friends of a Pure Gospel everywhere,' stating that at a special meeting of the Board of Trustees of the American Baptist Free Mission Society, held in Utica, N.Y., Dec. 15, 1847, the undersigned was invited to prepare a full statement of the origin, history, designs, and principles of the society -- an anti-slavery missionary body which admits no slaveholders and refuses fellowship with the compromising American Baptist Missionary Union. The officers and trustees are printed in full: President, Elder A. Post, Montrose, Pa.; Vice-Presidents, Dr. J. Trevor, Wm. A. Tweed Dale, Elder S. White, New York; Deacon Wm. Goding, Massachusetts; Elder M. D. Miller, Vermont; Elder A. T. Foss, New Hampshire; J. W. Sawyer, H. Hawes, Maine; George Lyon, Connecticut; Elder Wm. H. Brisbane, New Jersey; Samuel Aaron, Pennsylvania; Elder W. Walker, Illinois; Elder E. Matthews, Wisconsin. Trustees: Elders W. Tillinghast, S. S. Hayward, E. R. Warren, Brethren George Curtis, J. H. Sterry, L. Lawrence, Z. Brockett, J. Prescott, J. T. Quaiffe, J. B. Price, Isaac S. Ford. Auditors: A. J. Stone, Francis Childs. Corresponding Secretary: Elder C. P. Grosvenor, Utica, N.Y. Recording Secretary: George F. Post, New Berlin, N.Y. Treasurer: John N. Barbour, Boston, Mass. Assistant Treasurer: George Curtiss, Utica, N.Y. The society's one foreign mission is in the republic of Hayti: two missionary families at Port-au-Prince consisting of Elders Wm. M. Jones and -- L. Judd (first initial obscured; probably W. L. Judd) and their wives, together with Misses P. T. Young and E. Lake (surname partly obscured); in the home field it aids missions among the fugitives in Canada and employs agents and colporteurs in the West. The statement is signed E. R. Warren, Gen. Ag't Am. Free Mis. Soc'y, Albany, Dec., 1847.
